# Alcohol-associated liver disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the liver > Alcohol-associated liver disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/5S0iZf)

---

## Summary

<u>Alcohol</u>-associated <u>liver</u> disease (ALD) refers to a spectrum of progressive <u>liver</u> conditions caused by chronic <u>harmful alcohol use</u>. One-third of the US population exceed <u>moderate alcohol consumption</u>, increasing their risk of ALD. Early ALD is typically asymptomatic and manifests with potentially reversible <u>alcohol-associated steatosis</u> or <u>steatohepatitis</u>. Continued <u>alcohol</u> consumption may lead to <u>alcohol-associated hepatitis</u>, which is characterized by acute <u>jaundice</u>, <u>malaise</u>, and <u>fever</u>. Patients with advanced ALD may develop <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>cirrhosis</u>. <u>Patient history</u>, <u>transaminase</u> levels, and imaging are used to determine the stage of ALD. Management of ALD requires complete cessation of <u>alcohol</u> consumption.




The management of <u>alcohol-associated hepatitis</u>, including its diagnosis and treatment, is described in detail in “<u>Alcohol-associated hepatitis</u>.” The management of <u>alcohol</u>-related <u>cirrhosis</u> is described in “<u>Cirrhosis</u>.”

## Overview

| <br>Overview of <u>alcohol</u>-associated <u>liver</u> disease [[1]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[2]](/library/dkdo5J0)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Clinical features | Pathology | Typical disease course |
| Alcohol-associated steatosis | <br><br>* Usually asymptomatic<br><br>* Some patients report a sensation of pressure in the upper abdominal area.<br><br>* In some cases, <u>hepatomegaly</u>: soft consistency<br><br><br> | <br>* Accumulation of lipid droplets in <u>hepatocytes</u> with gradual single-cell <u>necrosis</u> within the lobules<br><br> | <br><br>* May be reversible after cessation of <u>alcohol</u> consumption<br><br>* Acute exacerbation and risk of hepatic failure are rare.<br><br>* May progress to <u>alcohol-associated steatohepatitis</u> and <u>liver fibrosis</u> if <u>alcohol</u> consumption continues<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Alcohol-associated hepatitis</u> [[3]](/library/iOdJHJ0)<br> | <br><br>* Acute <u>jaundice</u><br><br>* <u>Fever</u><br><br>* Tender <u>hepatomegaly</u><br><br>* <u>Malaise</u><br><br>* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>anorexia</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Macrovesicular <u>steatosis</u> with hydropic swelling and ballooning degeneration of <u>hepatocytes</u> within the lobules<br><br>* Damaged <u>hepatocytes</u> typically contain <u>Mallory-Denk bodies</u> (<u>hyaline</u> <u>inclusion bodies</u> that contain <u>keratin</u> filaments and appear eosinophilic on <u>HE staining</u>).<br><br>* Immunoreaction: <u>neutrophilic granulocytes</u> within hepatic tissue<br><br>* Pericellular and sinusoidal <u>fibrosis</u><br><br>* Pronounced excess formation of fibrous collagenous <u>connective tissue</u><br><br>* Chicken wire-like network in perivenous zones<br><br>* Mechanical obstruction of the <u>bile</u> ducts and biliary stasis<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Reversible in mild cases<br><br>* Progression of <u>liver fibrosis</u> is accelerated.<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Alcohol</u>-associated <u>cirrhosis</u> [[4]](/library/kIYm1q)<br> | <br><br>* Final stage of ALD<br><br>* Asymptomatic in the early stage<br><br>* Fatigue, weight loss, abdominal distention, <u>spider angiomata</u><br><br>* <u>Decompensated cirrhosis</u>: bleeding <u>varices</u>, <u>ascites</u>, <u>encephalopathy</u>, <u>jaundice</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Infiltration of <u>lymphocytes</u><br><br>* Massive accumulation of fat in <u>hepatocytes</u><br><br>* Formation of fibrous septa and regenerative <u>nodules</u><br><br>* Perivascular <u>sclerosis</u> of <u>central veins</u> (especially in the early stage)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Irreversible<br><br>* <u>Liver transplantation</u> is the only definitive treatment option.<br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Alcohol-associated steatosis</u> and mild <u>alcohol-associated hepatitis</u> may be reversible after cessation of <u>alcohol</u> consumption. However, <u>severe alcohol-associated hepatitis</u> and <u>cirrhosis</u> are irreversible.

## Etiology

### <u>Alcohol</u>-related <u>risk factors</u> [[1]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[2]](/library/dkdo5J0)




* <u>Alcohol use disorder</u>

* <u>Harmful alcohol use</u>, especially if consumed from a young age and for individuals in their 40s or 50s

* Men: ≥ 3 drinks per day or ≥ 21 per week

* Women: ≥ 2 drinks per day or ≥ 14 per week

* <u>Binge drinking</u>

* Drinking outside of meal times

* Drinking daily

* See “<u>Classifications of alcohol use</u>” for definitions and types of <u>alcohol</u> consumption.





### Non-<u>alcohol</u>-related <u>risk factors</u> [[1]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[2]](/library/dkdo5J0)




* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>MASLD</u>

* <u>Hepatitis B</u>

* <u>Hepatitis C</u>

* Tobacco use

* Female sex

* Hispanic or Native American descent

* Low <u>socioeconomic status</u>

* Certain genetic variants





> [!TIP]
> Coffee consumption may reduce the risk of ALD in individuals with <u>heavy alcohol use</u>. [[2]](/library/dkdo5J0)

---

## Pathophysiology

* Hepatic <u>degradation of ethanol</u> to <u>acetyl-CoA</u> by <u>alcohol dehydrogenase</u> results in <u>NADH</u> excess (see <u>breakdown of ethanol</u> for more details) → ↑ <u>NADH</u> drives the formation of <u>glycerol 3-phosphate</u> (<u>G3P</u>) from <u>dihydroxyacetone phosphate</u> (<u>DHAP</u>) → ↑ in both <u>G3P</u> and <u>fatty acids</u> causes increased <u>triglyceride synthesis</u> in the <u>liver</u> and accompanying inflammation → <u>steatohepatitis</u> → <u>chronic inflammation</u> leads to <u>hepatic fibrosis</u> and <u>sclerosis</u> → <u>portal hypertension</u> and eventually <u>cirrhosis</u>

## Diagnosis

See “<u>Diagnostics for cirrhosis</u>” and “<u>Diagnosis of alcohol-associated hepatitis</u>” for more detailed approaches to those manifestations of ALD.




### Approach [[1]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[2]](/library/dkdo5J0)




* Screen individuals with <u>harmful alcohol use</u> for ALD using <u>laboratory studies</u> and <u>liver</u> <u>ultrasound</u>.

* ALD diagnosis requires:

* ≥ 12 months of <u>harmful alcohol use</u>

* Typical clinical, laboratory, and/or imaging findings of <u>liver</u> disease

* Exclusion of alternative causes of <u>liver</u> disease (e.g., viral <u>hepatitis</u>, <u>autoimmune hepatitis</u>, <u>hemochromatosis</u>)

* In individuals with asymptomatic ALD, evaluate the severity of <u>liver fibrosis</u> using noninvasive tests.





### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[1]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[2]](/library/dkdo5J0)




* Early ALD

* <u>Elevated transaminases</u>

* ↑ <u>ALT</u> and ↑ <u>AST</u> (typically < 400 U/L) [[2]](/library/dkdo5J0)

* <u>AST</u> > <u>ALT</u>

* ↑ <u>Alkaline phosphatase</u>

* <u>Macrocytic anemia</u>  [[8]](/library/-nXDDA)

* ↑ Serum <u>ferritin</u> [[9]](/library/ikdJnJ0)

* Advanced ALD

* ↑ <u>Bilirubin</u>

* ↑ <u>PT</u> and <u>INR</u>

* ↓ <u>Albumin</u>

* <u>Thrombocytopenia</u>

* Direct <u>alcohol</u> biomarkers  [[1]](/library/y4ddNJ0)

* <u>Blood alcohol concentration</u>

* Urine and/or <u>hair</u> <u>ethyl glucuronide</u>

* Urine <u>ethyl sulfate</u>

* Blood <u>phosphatidylethanol</u>

* Indirect <u>alcohol</u> biomarkers

* ↑ <u>GGT</u>

* Indicates <u>alcohol</u>-induced tissue damage

* Highly variable and low <u>sensitivity</u> [[1]](/library/y4ddNJ0)

* ↑ <u>Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin</u>: low <u>sensitivity</u> and may be falsely positive in individuals with severe <u>liver</u> disease but no <u>alcohol</u> use





### Imaging [[10]](/library/QkdunJ0)




* <u>Ultrasound</u>: first line

* Mild <u>hepatomegaly</u>

* <u>Blood vessels</u> cannot be visualized.

* ↑ <u>Liver</u> <u>echogenicity</u> due to <u>steatosis</u>; may be focal or diffuse

* CT: ↓ <u>liver</u> attenuation





> [!NOTE]
> Imaging findings and laboratory study results will return to normal within weeks of cessation of <u>alcohol</u> consumption in patients with <u>alcohol-associated steatosis</u>. [[11]](/library/jkd_nJ0)

### Screening for <u>fibrosis</u> [[1]](/library/y4ddNJ0)[[2]](/library/dkdo5J0)




Screen individuals with asymptomatic ALD and consider screening individuals with <u>heavy alcohol use</u>.




* Noninvasive tests: preferred screening method

* <u>FIB-4 score</u>

* <u>Transient elastography</u>

* <u>Liver biopsy</u>: if there is diagnostic uncertainty after noninvasive tests

---

## Management

* Immediate cessation of <u>alcohol</u> consumption

* Multidisciplinary <u>management of AUD</u>

* Hepatology referral for individuals with advanced <u>liver fibrosis</u> or <u>cirrhosis</u>

* Treatment of <u>alcohol-associated hepatitis</u> and <u>treatment of cirrhosis</u> as indicated

* <u>Liver transplant</u> evaluation for patients with severe disease

---

## Complications

### <u>Decompensated cirrhosis</u>




Mainly characterized by a constellation of clinical features resulting from decreased <u>hepatic function</u>:




* <u>Portal hypertension</u>

* <u>Ascites</u>

* <u>Hepatic encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Coagulopathy</u>

* <u>Hepatorenal syndrome</u>

* <u>Hyperestrogenism</u>

* <u>End-stage liver disease</u>





### Other organ damage following chronic <u>alcohol</u> use




* <u>Gastritis</u>

* <u>Malabsorption</u>

* <u>Chronic pancreatitis</u>

* <u>Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome</u>

* See “<u>Alcohol use disorder</u>.”





### Zieve syndrome [[12]](/library/PkdWLJ0)




* A rare condition that can occur in individuals with ALD

* Characterized by the following triad:

* <u>Hemolytic anemia</u>

* <u>Jaundice</u>

* <u>Hyperlipidemia</u>





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
